title: Why are people trying to move the Bean? The 7-inch joke, explained
answer: Trying to move Chicago's Bean is a joke. An anonymous online invite asked Chicagoans to gather at Cloud Gate, the giant steel sculpture known as the Bean, on Nov. 8, 2026, and push it "seven inches to the left." Hundreds showed up, the 110-ton Bean didn't budge, and other cities, starting with St. Louis and its Gateway Arch, have copied the stunt.
body:
"Moving the Bean" means joining a crowd that pretends, with total seriousness, to shove a famous landmark a few inches. Nobody expects it to move; the fun is the group commitment, the countdown and the videos. Someone might post "we got it at least two inches, I felt it shift," or text a friend, "meet me at 12:47, wear gloves."

The idea started with a flyer and an event invite shared on Instagram ahead of Saturday, Nov. 8, 2026, calling for people to meet at Cloud Gate in Millennium Park at 12:47 p.m. and push the sculpture seven inches to the left. The invite came from a joke account and played on a made-up story that something, or someone, was hidden under the Bean; St. Louis Public Radio noted that rumors of a man trapped underneath were false. Hundreds of people turned up, leaned in and pushed. The Bean, which weighs about 110 tons, stayed exactly where it was.

It went viral because it was harmless, absurd and easy to copy. Videos of the Chicago push spread across TikTok and Instagram, and the city-rivalry angle did the rest. On Sunday, Nov. 15, a crowd in St. Louis tried to push the Gateway Arch "seven inches to the left" at 12:07 p.m., after a local social media account posted its own version of the flyer saying St. Louis was "stronger than Chicago." The Arch did not move either. ARTnews reported that Londoners were planning a similar push at Marble Arch.

For parents and teachers: this is one of the gentler internet trends. It is a meetup, not a dare, and there is nothing to learn about except crowd manners. The usual advice applies: stay with friends, don't climb on monuments, and leave the landmark as you found it.
in_the_news: After Chicago's Bean push on Nov. 8, 2026, St. Louis copied it at the Gateway Arch on Nov. 15, and searches for the joke jumped.

faq.a: No. Cloud Gate weighs about 110 tons and is fixed in place; the crowd's push was a joke and the sculpture stayed put.

faq.q: Why seven inches to the left?
faq.a: That was simply the goal written on the original Chicago invite. Later copycat events, like the one at the Gateway Arch, kept the same number.
An anonymous joke account shared the invite online. No official group or city agency was behind it.

faq.q: Did St. Louis move the Arch?
faq.a: No. Dozens of people tried at 12:07 p.m. on Nov. 15, 2026, mostly to one-up Chicago, and the Arch stayed where it was.
